messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan is a 61-year-old South Asian man who has been married for over thirty years and works as a program coordinator for a small non-profit focused on community health outreach. He was referred for psychological assessment approximately four months after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision in which the vehicle he was driving was struck broadside by a truck running a red light. The impact crumpled the passenger door inward, and Rajan was left pinned for nearly forty minutes before emergency services could extract him. During those minutes, his face was pressed against the torn fabric of the deflated airbag — a coarse, powdery texture he could neither escape nor ignore — while the sounds of traffic continuing to move around the wreck filled the air and bystanders shouted instructions he could not process. He was certain, during those forty minutes, that he was going to die.

In the weeks that followed, Rajan found that his memories of the event did not behave the way he expected memories to behave. Rather than fading with time, they arrived as vivid pictures — the angular crush of metal, the particular grey-white of the airbag fabric, the frozen moment of the truck filling his windshield. When those images surfaced, he did not experience them as recollections. He experienced them as repetitions. The terror he had felt pinned in the car returned with full physiological force — his chest tightened, his hands shook, and he was certain, in those moments, that the danger was present and immediate rather than past. This quality of reliving meant that the memories themselves functioned as a source of ongoing threat, and his nervous system responded accordingly: he became hypervigilant to any stimulus that might pull him back into that state.

The connection between the memories and his external world grew more intricate over time. Rajan found that the memories did not wait to be summoned — they could be triggered by encounters that carried the sensory signature of the collision. The coarse texture of certain upholstery fabrics, which he encountered regularly when visiting community centres and church halls as part of his outreach work, could return him instantly to the feeling of his face pressed against the airbag. The sight of a car with visible collision damage — common enough on city streets — produced the same effect, flooding him with the visual imagery of the crash. Conversations about road accidents, which arose with uncomfortable frequency among the older adults he served through his non-profit, would similarly pull the images forward. In each case, the trigger did not merely remind him of the event; it reinstated the memory in its full, present-tense terror.

What made the cycle particularly difficult to break was the way his heightened threat state fed back into the memory system itself. When Rajan was already on alert — startled by a sudden noise in a meeting room or by someone moving unexpectedly into his peripheral vision, both routine occurrences in his busy office — the arousal seemed to lower the threshold at which the intrusive images broke through. A door slamming in the corridor could send him into a state of hypervigilance, and from that state the visual memories arrived more readily, the reliving more complete. He had come to understand his own nervous system as unreliable and dangerous, a thing that could betray him into re-experiencing the worst moments of his life with no warning and no apparent exit.

Over months, Rajan quietly restructured his daily life around the anticipation of these episodes. He began driving different routes to avoid intersections where he might see damaged vehicles. He excused himself from conversations at work whenever the topic of accidents arose, offering thin explanations that his colleagues accepted without question, though he noticed their puzzled looks accumulating. His wife had observed the changes with growing concern — the flinching, the withdrawal, the nights he spent sitting awake. It was she who finally persuaded him to seek help. What Rajan most fears, as he begins treatment, is that the memories have become permanent — that the accident has rewritten something fundamental in him that cannot be undone. What he most hopes is that he is wrong.
